article.standfirst: One season as a Major Partner, and Penrite has bought the top slot at Melbourne.
body: Penrite Oil is now a principal partner of Melbourne's AFL and AFLW programs for the next two years, with its logo in two locations across both sets of playing guernseys in 2027. The club calls it the biggest commercial partnership in its 168-year history. No fee has been disclosed, so the size of the cheque stays a guess.

The more interesting part is how fast it moved. Penrite arrived ahead of the 2026 season as a Major Partner of the AFL side on a two-year term, with its logo on the top front and back of the guernsey. Later in 2026 it extended to the AFLW program, again as a Major Partner, with its logo on the back of the AFLW guernseys. A year on, it steps up to principal across both. That is a brand using a trial season as a live audition, then buying the top slot once it has seen what the footy audience does for it.

What Penrite is buying is guernsey space on two programs, and one of the best-known community days on the Victorian calendar. It is the new partner of the Walk to the 'G, the march to the MCG for FightMND ahead of the King's Birthday match against Collingwood. Melbourne CEO Dan Taylor said: "To have Penrite come on as our new Walk to the 'G partner speaks volumes of the quality of their company and their people." Penrite CEO Toby Dymond said the company is "particularly proud to come on board as the partner of the Walk to the 'G, supporting the incredible work of FightMND."

What the club gets is a principal partner across men's and women's football, and a story that suits both sides. Penrite was founded in Melbourne in 1926, so 2026 is its centenary, and it still describes itself as Australian-owned and family-owned. A local brand turning a hundred and putting its name on a Melbourne jumper is an easy narrative for a club to tell.

It also fits what Penrite has been building. Motorsport is its home base. It is Official Oil of Supercars and naming-rights partner of the Sandown 500 through at least 2027, after a multi-year extension announced in November 2025, and it is the exclusive event oil partner of five Supercars events, including the Bathurst 1000. It first joined Supercars in 2017. In July 2026 it added the Perth Bears as Major Foundation Partner and top back jersey sponsor, which was its debut in elite rugby league. Add the Demons and Penrite now sits across racing, rugby league and Australian rules inside a single year.

For the category, that matters. Oil and lubricant brands have traditionally spent their sponsorship money where engines are. Putting principal-level money onto a footy jumper is a bet that team sport reaches more of the people who buy oil than another livery does, particularly the fans who are also weekend car owners and mechanics. It is also a clean example of the step-up model: start as a Major Partner, prove the return, then take the front seat.

What to watch next: the 2027 guernsey reveal and exactly where the two Penrite positions land, how Penrite activates the Walk to the 'G on King's Birthday, and whether the AFLW side gets equal billing in the campaign. Also worth watching is whether the Perth Bears and Melbourne arrive in the same Penrite campaigns, because a brand with racing, league and footy partnerships has a lot of content to cross over.
article.close: A trial season, then the top of the Demons' partnership list.

features.label: Data drop
features.headline: Few sponsors cross the AFL-NRL line.
features.descriptor: Brand overlap across 33 AFL and NRL clubs

article.standfirst: Across 33 AFL and NRL clubs we count 1,129 sponsor brands, and only 74 of them back both codes.
body: Footy's two big codes chase the same Australian fans, but their sponsors rarely overlap. We took the current partner lists for 17 AFL clubs and 16 NRL clubs from the Parade database and counted every brand once per club. The AFL clubs list 462 different brands and the NRL clubs list 741. Put them together and you get 1,129 brands. Only 74 of them appear in both codes, which is about 7 per cent.

Those 74 punch above their weight. Between them they fill 293 of the 1,467 partner slots across the 33 clubs, or 20 per cent. So the brands that cross the line are the big, broad-reach names, while the rest of the list is sold code by code and club by club.

McDonald's is the clearest case. It sits at eight AFL clubs and eight NRL clubs, 16 in all. The Brisbane Lions announced a five-year extension to 2030, with McDonald's as Premier Partner of the men's team. Over in the NRL, the One New Zealand Warriors announced on 1 November 2026 that McDonald's had joined as official restaurant partner on a three-year term.

Elastoplast splits just as evenly, with six AFL clubs and six NRL clubs. The Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs named it official sports tape partner for the 2025 season, for at least two seasons, and the Warriors renewed it for two more years in December 2025. Gatorade is the biggest name on the shared list at 17 clubs, but it is an AFL story first: 15 AFL clubs list it, against two in the NRL (the Dolphins and the Warriors). The Warriors made it Official Hydration Partner from the 2025 season.

Eleven of the 74 shared brands sit at three or more clubs in each code. Between them, McDonald's, Gatorade and Elastoplast reach 27 of the 33 clubs. For a brand wanting both fan bases, the club-by-club route is slow, and few have done it.

A few limits apply. Port Adelaide, Parramatta and Tasmania are left out because their partner pages gave us ten names or fewer at the last check, and Perth Bears are out until they play. Every club included was checked between 2 and 10 November 2026. NRL clubs list more small suppliers than AFL clubs, so read the overlap as a guide, not a league table. Brands are counted as named, and the figures cover our database, not the whole market.
article.close: Few brands pay twice to reach footy fans.

features.label: Feature
features.headline: Youi sponsors the fans.
features.descriptor: Inside the insurer's NRL, AFL and cricket playbook

article.standfirst: From NRL referees in 2017 to five Big Bash clubs this summer, Youi has built one of Australian sport's most consistent partnership portfolios around one idea: the fans.
body: Youi is the Australian arm of South Africa's OUTsurance. It was set up here in 2008 and is still headquartered at Sippy Downs on the Sunshine Coast. It is now the engine of the group, with Australia making up about 65 per cent of OUTsurance's 2025 property and casualty premium, and it is still growing quickly: in the six months to December 2025, Youi Direct's gross written premium rose 23.8 per cent in Australian dollar terms.

That growth explains the sport spend. Youi sells direct, and in July 2025 it stopped writing new business through its broker channel, Blue Zebra Insurance. With no brokers in the mix, the brand has to do the selling. Youi has led the insurance category for total advertising spend, and it says it judges its partnerships on brand measures such as consideration and ad awareness rather than direct response.

The portfolio started with the people nobody cheers for. In February 2017 Youi signed as official partner of the NRL referees, with its brand on the officials' main branding spot, and later that year it took the same idea to the 2017 Rugby League World Cup, on referee apparel at all 40 men's and women's matches. Youi has been the NRL's Official Insurance Partner ever since. It joined the Brisbane Lions in 2020, and a five-year extension from 1 November 2024 made it the club's Principal Partner through to 2029 across the men's, women's, academy and community programs. From the 2025 season it also went on the front of the Lions AFLW guernsey, for five seasons.

What ties it together is one platform. In May 2024 Youi launched Footy. Made by Fans. across its NRL and Lions partnerships, built by its in-house creative team. It then handed its Lions sponsorship to a supporter, Scott Villiers, for Round 21. The Lions wore an away guernsey with his name where the Youi logo usually sits against St Kilda at Marvel Stadium on 4 August 2024, with M&C Saatchi Sport & Entertainment on content and PR. In 2026 the idea moved into the stadium itself, with the Youi Fan House behind the eastern goals at the Gabba, open to members and non-members alike.

2026 has been its biggest year yet. At Magic Round, Youi and the Australian Rugby League Commission launched Kick for a Cause with all 17 NRL clubs, aiming to raise $1 million for kids' cancer care, with Youi pledging $1,000 for every converted try and penalty goal and double for field goals. For State of Origin it built Youi Origin Verified with the NRL, a game where fans earned verified status through trivia and code-word challenges and were ranked from Bandwagoners to The Immortal. It drew 136,487 unique visitors, 259,175 page views and 26,832 unique entries, and the top fan won a trip to Origin Game 2 at Eden Park in 2027. Youi was also one of SBS's official broadcast partners for the FIFA World Cup.

Then came the big stages. In July Youi was named a Major Partner of the 2026 Rugby League World Cup, which ran from 15 October to 15 November across Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea and finished with the men's and women's finals at Suncorp Stadium. In late October it moved into cricket, as an official partner of the KFC BBL and Weber WBBL and on the kit of five clubs: Brisbane Heat, Hobart Hurricanes, Melbourne Renegades, Melbourne Stars and Sydney Thunder. It is also on umpire uniforms in both competitions. Note the wording in that launch. Marketing chief Angela Greenwood said Youi believes sport is made by fans. The footy line now covers every code Youi backs.

The SSS take: Youi owns an idea rather than a code. Referees, a fan on the jumper, a fan zone, a fan leaderboard and the umpires at the Bash all point back to the same message, which is hard to do when a brand sits across three sports. The Queensland base helps too, with a home club the Lions now bill as three-peat premiers and Magic Round, Origin and a World Cup final all in Brisbane. The pressure point is claims. Higher storm claims and weaker CTP results pushed Youi Group's claims ratio from 58.5 per cent to 62.2 per cent in the year to June 2026, and tighter margins tend to land on marketing budgets.
What to watch: whether the cricket deal grows beyond five clubs, how Youi activates around Origin at Eden Park in 2027, and the Lions partnership, which runs to 2029.
article.close: Footy made by fans is now sport made by fans. Expect the list to keep growing.

features.label: Feature
features.headline: The caps on private equity in sport.
features.descriptor: Each US league's limit, side by side

article.standfirst: Arctos's Falcons stake is the latest sale, and every US league has set its own limit on how much of a team private equity can own.
body: On 20 October, NFL owners approved private equity firm Arctos buying 7.5 per cent of the Atlanta Falcons, with a further 2.5 per cent committed subject to a separate owners' vote. Arctos joins as a limited partner, and the club says it is now a KKR business after KKR acquired it in 2026. Owner Arthur Blank, who holds about 73 per cent of the team, said the sale proceeds will go to his family's philanthropic causes. It is the latest in a run of stake sales that has put one firm in several NFL teams.

That run is easy to track. Arctos holds 8 per cent of the Chargers and 10 per cent of the Bills, and NFL owners approved a 3 per cent Browns stake at their May meeting in Orlando. The Falcons would make it four NFL teams. What caps how far that can go depends on the league, because each one wrote its own rulebook.

The NFL is the tightest. Owners voted in August 2024, at a special meeting in Minnesota, to let approved firms buy up to 10 per cent of a team. Each fund has to take at least 3 per cent, each purchase must be held for at least six years, and a fund can invest in up to six teams. Arctos, Ares Management and Sixth Street were among the firms approved.

The NBA is looser. From 3 December 2025 a financial investor can hold passive stakes in up to eight teams, up from five. A single investor can own up to 20 per cent of a team, and investors together are capped at 30 per cent. The NHL has run on much the same numbers since 2021: up to 30 per cent of a team can go to private firms in total, one firm can hold up to 20 per cent, and a firm can be in up to five teams.

MLB has just moved. Front Office Sports reported on 22 September that owners lifted the per-firm cap from 15 per cent to 20 per cent. Per that report the vote happened over the summer and was not publicly announced, and the source was unnamed. If a team's controlling owner holds less than 20 per cent, the cap drops to match that owner's stake. There is no limit on how many teams one firm can invest in.

Put side by side, the NFL's 10 per cent single-investor cap is half the 20 per cent allowed in the NBA, NHL and MLB. For brands and rights holders, the practical point is who sits in the register. A team with an institutional investor has a new audience for its commercial numbers, which makes sponsorship and media revenue part of how that stake gets judged. That is analysis, not something the leagues have said.

Why the caps matter more than any single stake: they set the ceiling on how much outside money a league can absorb, and who gets to compete for it. A 10 per cent limit with a six-year hold favours patient funds that take small slices of many teams. A 20 per cent limit with no cap on team numbers, as in MLB, leaves room for larger positions and wider portfolios. Neither says anything about price, and none of the sources above gives a valuation for these stakes, so this piece doesn't either.

The pattern across all four leagues is passive money. The rules talk about minority, non-controlling holders, and controlling owners keep running their clubs. That is the line that keeps the model acceptable to owners and fans alike, and each league adjusts the numbers without removing it. MLB's latest move was reported as matching the NBA's approach.
Two things worth watching: the vote on the extra 2.5 per cent of the Falcons, and whether the NFL ever shifts its 10 per cent line toward the other leagues.
article.close: Ten per cent in the NFL, twenty in the NBA, NHL and MLB, and the lines keep moving.

features.label: Breakdown
features.headline: Why ARN doubled down on tennis.

article.standfirst: ARN has locked in five years as the Australian Open's audio partner, and the value is still under wraps.
body: ARN and Tennis Australia have signed a five-year partnership that makes ARN the Australian Open's audio partner and broadcaster from the January 2027 tournament. It was announced on 11 November at ARN's Upfronts. Neither side has put a value on it. The scope runs across radio, iHeart, video, social and live experiences.

It is a renewal with a bigger commitment attached. ARN first partnered with the AO for the January 2023 tournament, then extended in November 2023 for three more years, through to after the 2026 event. By 2025 the activation included AO Radio on iHeart and entertainment partner roles at Riverside Social and Courtside Bar. Moving from three-year terms to five is the change. ARN Chief Content Officer Kerri Elstub called it "a huge commitment and a major step up from where we've been."

What ARN is buying is presence on site. Its biggest shows will broadcast from Melbourne Park, starting with KIIS and GOLD Breakfast and running through the workday into Drive with Carrie Bickmore, Jonesy and Amanda, and Smallzy. Eddie McGuire and Abbey Gelmi deliver updates on GOLD Sport. Around that sit a dedicated AO DAB+ channel in Sydney and Melbourne, live streaming on iHeart, and podcasts including Two Good Sports and the AO's official podcast, Pod Laver Arena. Coverage also goes out through ARN's regional network, and the ARE Media relationship stretches the package into food, fashion and lifestyle titles including ELLE and Gourmet Traveller.

The commercial logic sits in ARN's own numbers. Variety reports that ARN holds about 25 per cent of the metro radio audience but about 18.5 per cent of metro ad revenue, with CEO Michael Stephenson putting each share point at roughly $6 million and the full gap at around $38 million. A tournament that fills Melbourne Park every January gives the sales team a headline property to build packages around, and Elstub's comment that it means more advertiser opportunities points the same way. Mumbrella's read is that it is a major win for ARN, given the focus Seven and Nine have on sporting rights.

For Tennis Australia, the property is in good shape. The AO26 tournament, from 12 January to 1 February 2026, drew a record 1,368,043 fans over three weeks, up from 1,218,831 in 2025. Chief Commercial Officer Cedric Cornelis said the organisation was "delighted to welcome ARN as a long-term partner", and he framed ARN's daily reach as a way to bring tournament moments to fans in new ways. A partner committing for five years also gives the AO a stable audio line-up.

For ARN this is a summer plan with the AO at the centre. B&T reports content and commercial opportunities across the summer, before and after the tournament, so the partnership is built to run for weeks rather than a fortnight. That is a different shape from a one-off naming or signage partnership, and it suits a radio group that sells time and talent.

What to watch next: how ARN packages the AO for advertisers once the value is out in the market, how the DAB+ channel and iHeart streams perform in their first January under the new term, and whether the regional rollout and ARE Media tie-ins turn into products that agencies actually buy. The first real test is January 2027.
article.close: Five years, one tournament, and a radio group betting that January belongs to it.

article.standfirst: Across 17 AFL clubs we count 466 sponsor brands, and 403 of them back one club only.
body: Footy sponsorship looks like a crowded market, but the overlap between clubs is tiny. We took the current partner lists for 17 AFL clubs from the Parade database and counted every brand once per club. The clubs hold 615 partner slots between them, filled by 466 different brands. Of those brands, 403 appear at a single club. That is 86 per cent.

The brands that do cross club lines are a short list, and the top of it is all drinks. Gatorade shows up at 15 of the 17 clubs, Cool Ridge at 14 and Pepsi Max at 11. Together those three fill 40 slots. Behind them come New Era at nine clubs and McDonald's at eight. St Kilda's partner page is a good example: it carries Gatorade, Cool Ridge Water and Pepsi Max side by side.

McDonald's is the biggest non-drink name on the shared list. It sits at eight clubs, and Fremantle's own announcement calls it Official Quick Service Restaurant and Official Café of the Dockers for the AFL and AFLW teams. The pattern is clear enough: the brands that travel are everyday consumer names that want reach across footy's whole fan base, while the rest of the list is sold club by club.

Zoom out and 63 brands sit at two or more clubs, and between them they fill 212 of the 615 slots, or about 34 per cent. Only 28 brands reach three clubs and nine reach five. Everything else is a club-by-club partnership, from a local brewery to a car maker to a cyber security firm. For a brand, that means a club partnership rarely comes with a rival sitting next door on the same list.

Rosters differ a lot in size. Geelong lists 50 partners and Brisbane 48, while Fremantle sits at 27. The average is 36 per club. The numbers move with how fully each club lists its suppliers and smaller partners, so read the totals as a guide to scale, not a league table.

A few limits apply. Brands are counted as named, so Melbourne Airport and Melbourne Airport Parking are separate entries. Port Adelaide is left out because its partner page gave us only eight names at the last check, and Tasmania is out until it plays. Every club included was checked between 2 and 8 November 2026. The figures cover our database, not the whole market.
article.close: Share a sponsor with your rival and you are the exception.

features.label: Feature
features.headline: How Australia's national teams get paid.
features.descriptor: How the Socceroos and Matildas split the money

article.standfirst: A court action, a late payment and an agreement that expires in 2027 all point at how the Socceroos and Matildas share the money.
body: Two stories about Football Australia broke within a week of each other, and they circle the same question. On 3 November, AAP reported that Socceroos and Matildas players, acting through their union Professional Footballers Australia (PFA), had launched action against Football Australia (FA) in the NSW Supreme Court. Three days later, the ABC reported that Socceroos who played at the World Cup were still waiting on their match fees. Both come back to how a national team's money reaches the players.

Start with what is actually known about the court action, because it isn't much. AAP says the PFA is understood to be pursuing a seven-figure claim and is expected to argue that the revenue-sharing agreement is not being serviced properly. The PFA declined to comment. FA says the Supreme Court action relates to a third party in connection with a separate matter before the National Dispute Resolution Chamber, that the court's role is limited to the subpoena process, and that it will not comment further. Nothing has been decided, and the detail of any dispute hasn't been made public.

The model sitting behind it is worth understanding. Revenue sharing started with the 2019 agreement, which gave players 24 per cent of national team generated revenue in 2019/20 and added a percentage point each year of the four-year agreement. The current agreement, announced on 8 November 2023 and covering 2023 to 2027, builds on that model and links player rewards to national team commercial growth. Matildas players moved off centralised contracts onto match and commercial payments. AAP and Reuters both reported the payments split as 70 per cent match fees and 30 per cent commercial payments, with at least 5 per cent of national team revenue set aside for youth national team programs.

For a sponsor, that is the part to take in. A brand that signs with a national team is buying into a revenue pool that players share in under a formula both sides agreed to. The 2023 agreement also created a joint committee of FA and the PFA focused on commercial opportunities, team brands and high-performance standards. That makes the way national team revenue is counted a commercial question as much as an industrial one, and it gives players a direct interest in how well the commercial program performs.

The governing body is under its own pressure. FA reported on 21 May 2026 that 2025 revenue hit a record of about $139.45 million and that it had posted a record net loss of $15.34 million, up from $8.5 million the year before. Chief executive Martin Kugeler said about one in five staff would go, with the senior national teams not affected, and called the rising losses "not a situation that is sustainable or acceptable". When revenue and losses are both climbing, every shared dollar gets looked at harder.

Then there is the payment problem. The ABC, using AAP copy, reported on 6 November that Socceroos who played at the 2026 World Cup had not been paid match fees three months after the tournament. FA blamed the need for final specialist advice on North American tax and withholding obligations, and said it is ready to pay once that is sorted. PFA chief executive Beau Busch called the situation unacceptable. Nothing in the reporting links this to the court action, so the two should be read as separate threads.

What comes next is the bigger commercial story. The ABC reports the current agreement is due to expire in September 2027, and that talks on new terms haven't started. The agreement in place covers the cycle through the FIFA Women's World Cup 2027, so its replacement will set the terms for everything after it. Every national team sponsor is funding a formula as well as a team, and that formula goes back on the table within the year.
article.close: Who gets what from a national team's sponsors is about to be renegotiated.

features.label: Breakdown
features.headline: Naming a stadium that doesn't exist.
features.descriptor: Generali, AC Milan and Inter, unpacked

article.standfirst: Generali has put its name on a stadium that won't open for roughly five years, and the fee behind it is still only a report.
body: AC Milan and Inter unveiled the Generali Stadium on 29 October: a ground of about 71,500 seats the two clubs plan to share in the San Siro area of Milan. Generali takes the naming rights and becomes Official Insurance Partner of both clubs. The insurer and the clubs call it one of the largest stadium naming rights partnerships in global sport. None of them has published a fee or a length.

Reports fill the gap, though not consistently. SportsPro and Sportcal report a fee of about €650m over 20 years, or roughly €32.5m a year. Il Sole 24 Ore reports the same €650m over 25 years, or about €26m a year. Until someone confirms it, the figure and the term are reports, not facts.

What Generali is buying is timing. Its release says it is a partner from day one of the project, and the clubs say construction is expected to begin in 2028, with the first match targeted for the 2031/32 season and subject to approvals. So the insurer gets its name on a project that is still in design, and on a 281,000 square metre regeneration of the San Siro area that goes with it. The brand rides every render, planning headline and construction milestone for years before anyone finds a seat.

Compare that with Juventus. Its ground only took the Allianz name in 2017, six years after opening. Allianz is another insurer, so the category fit is familiar. The difference is that Juventus sold a stadium fans already knew by another name. Milan's clubs are selling a name before there is a building to compare it with, and that is a cleaner pitch.

For the clubs, it is one sale covering two fan bases. Sportcal reports they bought the stadium from the City of Milan in November 2025 for just under €197m, a figure SportsPro also gives, after a 2025 agreement with the city. The Milan release names RedBird and Oaktree as making a defining investment in the project. A naming partner signed this early gives that project a major commercial backer before construction starts. The Official Insurance Partner role also gives Generali a reason to be visible at both clubs in the meantime.

It is a step up from the rest of Generali's sport. The group's release points to the Davis Cup by Generali, the Barcolana sailing regatta it has backed for more than forty years, and running events across Europe including the Berlin Marathon. It became the partner behind the Davis Cup by Generali in September, per Sportcal. Those are events and competitions. A stadium name is a different kind of asset: permanent and shared between two rivals. Generali says it chose to back the two Italian clubs from the start because the group has long represented Italy internationally, and it reported premium income of €98.1bn in 2025 across more than 50 countries.

What to watch next is short. The approvals, because the 2031/32 target depends on them. Whether the fee and term are ever confirmed. And what the clubs sell around a name this size, since a shared stadium hands every other category the same two-club pitch. For anyone selling naming rights on a venue that isn't built yet, this is the template to study.
article.close: The name goes up first. The building follows.

features.label: Data drop
features.headline: ANZ sport runs on renewals.
features.descriptor: Renewals and extensions, ANZ v global, 2026

article.standfirst: Almost three in ten ANZ partnerships in our 2026 database are a renewal or extension. Globally it is fewer than one in five.
body: This one comes straight from the Parade database. We have logged 1,418 partnerships with an announcement date between 1 January and 3 November 2026: 679 in Australia and New Zealand and 739 global. It is what we have logged, not every partnership in the market, so read it as a comparison inside one database, not a census.

Of the 679 ANZ partnerships, 198 were renewals or extensions (141 renewals and 57 extensions). That is 29.2%. Of the 739 global partnerships, 140 were renewals or extensions, or 18.9%. Roughly 10 points separate the two. Put another way, about 29 in every 100 ANZ partnerships we logged this year kept an existing partner in place, against about 19 in every 100 globally.

It is not one big month skewing the result. Across January to October, the ANZ share sat more than a point above the global share in eight of the ten months. March and June were level. The same gap shows up in 2025: 37.2% of ANZ partnerships logged (176 of 473) were renewals or extensions, against 23.0% globally (116 of 504). Two different years, the same direction, which is why we are comfortable calling it a pattern in our data rather than a blip.

The codes tell different stories. Among ANZ partnerships this year, motorsport sits at 43.6% (17 of 39), football at 38.0% (27 of 71) and the AFL at 35.2% (43 of 122). The NRL is the outlier at 19.8%, just 19 of 96. Of the ANZ sports with 40 or more partnerships logged, it has the lowest renewal share. Motorsport's sample is small, so treat that one lightly. The data can't tell us why the NRL differs.

Recent examples show what the label covers. AGL renewed with Melbourne Victory on 22 October as Major Partner and Official and Exclusive Energy Partner for a further two seasons, to the end of 2027/28. Gazley renewed with the Wellington Phoenix on 30 October for 2026-27, covering the men's and women's teams. Geely Auto Australia extended with the Bulldogs for 2027 and 2028, announced on 2 November.
For brands, the takeaway is that in most ANZ codes the incumbent is often the partner to beat. For rights holders, a big slice of the sales year is keeping the logos already on the wall.
article.close: Count the renewals before you chase the new logos.

features.headline: What Australia's betting ban covers.
features.descriptor: The new rules for sport, from kit to live broadcasts

article.standfirst: A new federal law starts on 1 January 2027 and rewrites how betting money flows into Australian sport, but the logos will not vanish overnight.
body: Australia's wagering advertising reforms are due to start on 1 January 2027. They ban betting ads on playing kit, around grounds and through live sport coverage. The catch is a long runway for partnerships already signed, so the change will roll through the sport calendar over several years, not land in a single day.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced the package at the National Press Club on 2 April 2026. The Interactive Gambling Amendment (Gambling Reform) Bill 2026 then passed Parliament on 19 August after an agreement with the Coalition, and the Act received assent in late August. It stops short of the full ban on online gambling advertising that a 2023 parliamentary inquiry recommended.

The part that matters most to rights holders is the kit and venue rule. A licensed wagering provider cannot authorise or cause wagering advertising to appear on a player's or official's uniform, or at premises connected with a sporting event where the public can see it. The government's FAQ spells out the reach: on-field signage, external stadium signage, perimeter signage and even coaches' boxes. The civil penalty is 1,000 penalty units. Note where the duty sits. It lands on the bookmaker, not the club.

Broadcasts get their own rules. Wagering ads are banned on broadcast, datacast and online content services around live sport, from 15 minutes before the scheduled start until five minutes after the event ends, between 5am and 8:30pm. TV is capped at three betting ads an hour. Promoting odds is banned, and athletes, celebrities and influencers cannot front betting ads.

Racing is carved out. Under the Act a horse, harness or greyhound race is not treated as a sporting event, and the uniform and venue ban does not apply to it. The government's FAQ also exempts dedicated racing and wagering channels, programs and venues.

Now the transition, and read this part carefully. The government's April FAQ said existing partnerships would be honoured until they finish. Trade reports since the Act passed say existing sponsorships can run until 31 December 2031, a five-year window. Communications Minister Anika Wells said she would prefer clubs end betting ties early but left it to each organisation. Independent senator David Pocock called the delay absurd, and Liberal MP Andrew Wallace had pushed for two years. The Act also sets a statutory review three years after commencement.

Some sponsors were already heading for the exit. In 2024 PointsBet Australia CEO Andrew Catterall said stadium naming rights and perimeter signage were no longer appropriate for the category, and the company said it would not renew its naming rights at the Sharks' home ground when its partnership expired at the end of 2024.

Offshore, the Premier League shows how it can go. Its clubs agreed in April 2023 to pull gambling sponsors from the front of matchday shirts from the end of the 2025/26 season. Sky Sports reported eight clubs carried such sponsors, worth an estimated 60 million pounds a year. That move covered the front of the shirt only. The Australian rules reach kit, grounds and the broadcast.

The open question for brands is who fills the space. Alcohol is already everywhere. A report from the Foundation for Alcohol Research and Education found every AFL and NRL club had an alcohol sponsor as of May 2026. Rights holders sitting on betting partnerships now have a planning job: when each contract ends, what replaces it, and how to price kit, signage and broadcast inventory without the category.

Dates to watch are the 1 January 2027 start, the first clubs to walk away from their betting partnerships early, the first naming and perimeter partnerships signed in other categories, and the three-year review.
article.close: The first clubs to cut betting partnerships early will show what the replacement market is really paying.

features.headline: Inside the NRL's $5.3bn partnership.
features.descriptor: How the 2028 to 2034 rights partnership is carved up

article.standfirst: The NRL's seven-year, $5.3 billion rights partnership is the biggest in Australian sport. Here is who gets what.
body: The NRL's new broadcast partnership is worth $5.3 billion over seven years, from 2028 to 2034, and it is the biggest commercial agreement any Australian sport has signed. The league says cash per year jumps 90 per cent on the current arrangement. Spread evenly, that is about $757 million a season, against the more than $400 million a year the NRL announced when it signed the 2023 to 2027 partnership. By the same rough maths, the AFL's $4.5 billion partnership for 2025 to 2031 works out at $643 million a season.

The headline number gets the attention. The structure is where the value sits. There are three buyers and each gets a different slice. Foxtel Group, which is owned by DAZN, stays the home of the league across Foxtel and Kayo Sports. It shows every NRL and NRLW premiership match live, including the finals, other than State of Origin and the grand final.

Nine keeps the free-to-air crown jewels. It has exclusive coverage of the NRL Grand Final and of both the men's and women's State of Origin series. On top of that it simulcasts three NRL and NRLW games a week, so the pay-TV home and the free home show the same match at the same time. For a sponsor, that mix matters. Origin and the grand final deliver the mass audience on free TV, while the weekly simulcasts keep brand exposure steady across the season. Across the Tasman, Sky NZ will put more than 130 fixtures on its free platforms.

Then there is the world outside Australia and New Zealand. Foxtel has a revenue-sharing and marketing agreement on international rights, which excludes New Zealand and Papua New Guinea. Foxtel chief executive Patrick Delany says NRL content will reach 200 international markets through DAZN. ARLC chairman Peter V'landys has described going global as the priority once this partnership is done.

The partnership also changes who holds the pen. The Australian Rugby League Commission takes back control of season structure, scheduling and the draw. V'landys says that will mean fair scheduling for all clubs. He also says about 95 per cent of the money is cash and only 5 per cent contra, which is free advertising and promotion rather than dollars in the bank.

The growth built into the contract is just as important. Perth joins in 2027 as the 18th team, with the PNG Chiefs following in 2028. The NRL has told DAZN it will look at a 20th club around 2029, with New Zealand and Queensland the names in the frame. If that happens, Foxtel picks up an extra exclusive game each week. More games mean more inventory for sponsors, more reasons for fans to subscribe and more leverage for the league at the next renewal.

The rest of the market was circling. Seven and Amazon Prime Video were reported to have been interested, and Ten has been named too. The NRL went the other way on packaging. It kept a single pay-TV and streaming partner rather than splitting games across several services. NRL chief executive Andrew Abdo said the league could have put more content behind the paywall but went the other way. The open question is price, because fans will want to know if Kayo gets dearer. Delany says the entry-level Kayo price has risen only once in nearly nine years, and V'landys says he has protected the price point.

For brands and rights holders, the message is clear. Free-to-air reach is locked in for Origin and the grand final through 2034, the pay-TV rights are priced for growth, and the league now controls its own calendar. That gives sponsors seven years of certainty on where their logos will be seen, and gives clubs a stronger base to sell from. Nine's chief executive Matt Stanton has pointed to a commitment to bring the action live and free, and the NRL says its audience has roughly doubled over the past five years, so the pitch to brands is built on momentum as well as money. How much of that momentum survives a bigger, more expensive league is the real test.
article.close: Watch the 20th club decision, the Kayo price and whether DAZN can sell the NRL overseas, because those three will decide how the partnership ages.

features.headline: The NBA's most expensive square.
features.descriptor: How NBA jersey patches work and what they're worth

article.standfirst: An Australian-founded AI company now owns the priciest bit of fabric in American sport, and it's about six centimetres wide.
body: From this NBA season, IREN's logo sits on the front of every Golden State Warriors jersey. Sportico reported the multi-year partnership at more than US$50 million a year, which would make it the biggest sponsorship in North American team sport. IREN began in 2018 as Iris Energy, a Sydney-based bitcoin miner set up by brothers Will and Daniel Roberts, and now trades on Nasdaq as an AI cloud business. It replaces Rakuten, the Warriors' only patch partner until now, and also lands on the Santa Cruz Warriors' jerseys in the G League and the warmup tops of the WNBA's Golden State Valkyries.

So what are they actually buying? The NBA's board of governors signed off on jersey sponsorship in April 2016 as a three-year trial, starting with the 2017-18 season. The rules are tight: one logo, roughly 2.5 inches square, on the front left of the jersey opposite the Nike swoosh. Each club sells its own. The Philadelphia 76ers were first out of the blocks, announcing StubHub in May 2016. Compare that with an AFL or NRL jumper, where sponsors share the front, back and sleeves. The NBA went the other way and sold scarcity. One badge, one brand, on every game, every highlight clip and every replica jersey in the club shop.

Scarcity has done wonders for the price. When the Warriors signed Rakuten in 2017, the three-year, US$60 million partnership was the richest in the league. In 2021 the Lakers topped it, signing Korean food brand Bibigo on a five-year partnership reported by the LA Times at more than US$100 million. This June IREN's number blew both out of the water, and a month later ESPN reported the Lakers' new patch with finance app Albert at north of US$30 million a year. The trial has long since become a permanent fixture.

The 2026 off-season turned into a full reshuffle. In July the Dallas Mavericks signed JPMorganChase, the bank's first NBA patch, bundled with banking partner rights, a dedicated arena entrance for Chase cardholders and new community courts across North Texas. In September the Milwaukee Bucks swapped Motorola for Uline, a Wisconsin packaging supplier that has backed the club since 2013. The Phoenix Suns replaced PayPal with Paze, the digital wallet run by Early Warning Services, the company behind Zelle. The 76ers replaced Crypto.com with Bloom Energy, adding the Delaware Blue Coats' jerseys and a seven-figure charity investment. And in October Disney extended with the Orlando Magic, where it has been on the jersey since 2017, and added a Walt Disney World Atrium at Kia Center.

Look at who's buying. Blinkfire counted 29 of 30 teams with a patch in 2025-26, and financial brands were the biggest group with seven. This off-season the money moved again: crypto out in Philadelphia, energy in, and an AI infrastructure company paying the top price in the league. IREN sells GPU computing power to companies building AI, so it's buying credibility with a global business audience as much as fan awareness. The Warriors' own pitch is that the patch is their most visible global platform. A team in a big market with a global fan base can charge for that reach.

The patch also matters because of what hangs off it. The big ones are rarely just a logo. They come with named arena spaces, hospitality, cardholder perks, G League and WNBA rights, content and community programs. SponsorUnited put NBA team sponsorship revenue at US$1.62 billion in 2024-25, up 8% on the year before, with jersey patch partnerships more than doubling. Once the NBA proved the model, the rest of American sport followed. The NHL allowed jersey patches from 2022-23, and MLB from 2023, with the San Diego Padres first to sign, with Motorola.

For Australian rights holders, the lesson is in the pricing. The NBA didn't make more inventory, it made less, then let 30 clubs compete to sell the one spot that turns up in every photo. Fewer, bigger, better-defined assets with rights bundled around them is the same playbook any club can run, whether it's a sleeve, a training top or a naming right.

What to watch next: whether IREN's reported fee becomes the new benchmark when the next big-market patch comes up, and whether AI and energy brands keep replacing the finance and crypto money that defined the first decade of patches. Watch the activation too. A patch partnership that only ever shows up on the shirt is the easiest one to lose at renewal.
article.close: It's the smallest logo in the building, and the most expensive one.

features.headline: The AO's partner machine.
features.descriptor: Why the Australian Open keeps signing new brands

article.standfirst: Three partnerships in eight days, with AO 2027 less than three months away. Tennis Australia has turned sponsorship into a production line.
body: In the space of eight days this month, Tennis Australia signed DoorDash as the Australian Open's official on-demand delivery partner, named Adobe its official AI marketing and creativity partner, and locked Sky in as the tournament's New Zealand broadcaster through to 2032. Nobody put a number on any of the three. Together they show how the AO makes its money now: keep building new things to sell, then carve them into very specific categories.

Start with the categories. A footy club has a shirt front, a sleeve and some signage to flog. The AO's partner list reads more like a shopping centre directory. Kia has been the major partner since 2002. Emirates, Rolex and Luzhou Laojiao sit at associate level, with the Chinese baijiu maker on board since 2019. Below them runs a long tail of tightly defined partnerships: ANZ as official bank, Altos as official tequila in its Grand Slam debut, DiDi as ride share partner for AO 2026, and now DoorDash for delivery and Adobe for AI marketing. Because the partnerships are sold by category, every new category is extra money rather than a discount on an old one.

The bigger trick is making more event to sell. The AO now runs over three weeks, with an Opening Week in front of the main draw. In 2026 total attendance hit a record 1,368,043, up from 1,218,831 the year before. Opening Week alone pulled 217,999, nearly double 2025, on the back of open practice sessions, the first Opening Ceremony and the AO 1 Point Slam. Crowds also cracked 100,000 on four separate days for the first time. More days with people through the gates means more days a partner can activate, and the AO LIVE concerts, which ran five nights at John Cain Arena in 2026, stretch the precinct into the evening too.

The 1 Point Slam is the best example of inventory built from scratch. Amateurs and pros play single-point matches for a winner-takes-all $1 million. In January it ran on Rod Laver Arena as the AO 1 Point Slam Driven by Kia, and Jordan Smith, a 29-year-old NSW state champion, knocked out Jannik Sinner on his way to the cheque. For 2027 Haier has taken the sponsorship and the format has been pushed into clubs and schools around the country. Community winners feed into state championships in December, state winners play during Opening Week, and the champion's club gets a $50,000 grant. One property now gives a sponsor a grassroots program and a primetime moment.

The media money underwrites the lot. Nine holds the AO and the summer of tennis from 2025 to 2029 in a partnership Nine said carried a $425 million cash component, the biggest in Tennis Australia's history. Australians watched 149 million hours of the 2025 tournament across platforms, up 8 per cent, and the 2026 prize pool climbed 16 per cent to a record $111.5 million. Those audiences are what partners are really buying.

This month's partnerships show where the next dollar comes from. The Sky renewal adds New Zealand rights to the Laver Cup and United Cup, keeps every main draw match live on Sky's platforms and puts evening sessions on free-to-air Three and ThreeNow from 2027, extending a 25-year relationship. Adobe is a different beast. It's the software giant's first tennis sponsorship anywhere, and Tennis Australia will use Adobe CX Enterprise to show each fan the matches, food and activities most relevant to them. DoorDash plays the same game at the bar: from AO 2027, patrons at the Golden Hour Bar on Grand Slam Oval can order from selected vendors through DoorDash, an AO first. The partner becomes part of the plumbing, and the event runs better for it.

For rights holders the lesson travels well beyond Melbourne Park. The AO didn't sit around waiting for brands to want a bigger logo. It built new inventory, from Opening Week to a concert series to a $1 million novelty event, and gave partners a job inside it. For brands, the open door is the category list. If there's room for an official tequila and an official AI marketing partner, there's room for plenty more.
article.close: AO 2027 runs 11 to 31 January. Watch whether Opening Week grows again, and how many more 'official' partners land before the first ball.
